clue.text: Awful pity, having to confess to arson?

definitions.meaning: a crying shame, something deeply regrettable
whimsically, the shame felt by someone owning up to setting fires

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the idiom literally: the shame of a fire-raiser is quite literally about burning.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a deeply regrettable state of affairs, and the second reading is the embarrassment of a self-confessed fire-starter.

clue.text: Bow-wow! Frenzied din, breaking in through here!

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one set of letters goes into the dog's bark

parts.note: bow-wow is the conventional written bark of a dog

indicators.note: frenzied means wild and disordered, so the letters of din are jumbled

explanation.surface: A dog barks wildly as a burglar smashes in through the house's front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frenzied' scrambles the noise into IND, which 'breaking in' splits the dog's bark around. The definition is a burglar's way into the house, so the surface is almost a picture of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A curved projecting window is somewhere an intruder might climb in, so a housebreaker could get inside by that route.

clue.text: Arm moving up and down

indicators.note: in a down clue the word reads the same whether you go up the column or down it

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Someone's limb is pumping up and down, perhaps in exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a palindrome, so in a down entry it reads the same upwards as downwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotor is the spinning arm of a machine such as a helicopter or a car's distributor.

clue.text: Unusual idiom, it's portrayal of a moronic state

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters of the words that follow are put into an unfamiliar order

parts.note: it's is short for it is, giving the letters I, T, S

explanation.surface: A linguist remarks that an odd turn of phrase makes the speaker sound foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' shuffles IDIOM with ITS. 'portrayal of a' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiotism is an old word for idiocy, the condition of being utterly foolish.

clue.text: Cackling sound? It's all the geese!

definitions.meaning: the noise of geese honking and cackling together
a whole flock of geese gathered on the ground

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to cackle like geese; as a noun it is the collective term for a flock of those birds.

clue.text: Will be rough on a penitent

definitions.text: Will be rough on a penitent

parts.words: Will be rough on a penitent
parts.note: describes a garment of coarse cloth worn next to the skin as self-punishment by someone doing penance

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' sounds like harsh treatment, but it is literal: the garment is scratchy and worn on the penitent's body.
explanation.definitionFit: Penitents once wore a coarse shirt of goat's hair under their clothes to mortify the flesh.

clue.text: Low about race slogan

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so the cow's noise goes round the race

parts.note: to low is to moo, the sound a cow makes
the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A downbeat comment on a race's catchphrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like an adjective but is the cow's call MOO, which goes 'about' TT.
explanation.definitionFit: A motto is a short phrase summing up a principle, much like a slogan.

clue.text: Anxious on losing a ring, English snob's off-putting such dislikeable behaviour!

indicators.note: putting something off its normal course scrambles it, so all these letters are rearranged
losing means the following letter is dropped from the word anxious

parts.note: a ring is round, like the letter O
the letters of snob plus the S from the possessive

explanation.surface: A nervous person dislikes a snob's offhand, unpleasant conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' drops A from ANXIOUS to leave NXIOUS; 'off-putting' then shuffles NXIOUS, O, E and SNOBS. 'on' is only a link, and 'off-putting' doubles as a surface adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Obnoxiousness is the quality of being highly unpleasant, the kind of conduct people find hateful.

clue.text: Order "get me nag!" to groom, when earlier assignment's required

parts.note: to preen is to groom oneself, as a bird tidies its feathers

indicators.note: to order things is to arrange them, so the letters in the quoted phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rider commands a stable lad to fetch and groom a horse because of a prior booking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a verb introducing the quoted speech, but it is the signal to rearrange those letters, which follow the word for grooming.
explanation.definitionFit: A pre-engagement is a commitment made beforehand, an assignment already accepted.

clue.text: Can be drawn and also plucked

definitions.text: Can be drawn and also plucked

parts.words: Can be drawn and also plucked
parts.note: describes the cord of an archer's weapon, pulled back to shoot and twanged like a harp string

explanation.walkthrough: 'drawn' suggests a picture and 'plucked' a chicken, but both describe the cord that an archer pulls back and lets go.
explanation.definitionFit: The cord of an archer's weapon is pulled back before release and can be twanged with the fingers.

clue.text: Brings the mission to a pause

definitions.text: Brings the mission to a pause

parts.words: Brings the mission to a pause
parts.note: a word meaning bury, placed before the word mission, makes a break between acts of a show

explanation.walkthrough: The word means to bury, but the clue plays on it as a prefix: written in front of MISSION it makes a word for an interval at the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Joined to the word in the clue it forms the name of a break in a play or film, a pause in proceedings.

clue.text: Tree, very large? That is right?

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, the clothing label for very large
i.e. abbreviates the Latin id est, meaning that is

explanation.surface: Someone queries whether a tree really is enormous.
explanation.walkthrough: OS (outsize) is a clothing-size label for very large garments.
explanation.definitionFit: An osier is a kind of willow, a tree whose pliant shoots are used in basketwork.

clue.text: Note the French range of optical equipment

parts.note: te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale
le is the French word for the
scope means extent or range

explanation.surface: A memo about a French firm's line of lenses and binoculars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'range' reads as a product line but is SCOPE, meaning extent.
explanation.definitionFit: A telescope is an optical instrument for magnifying distant objects.

clue.text: Neglected, yet appears in fresh undies

indicators.note: in places the verb inside the rearranged underwear
fresh means new or remade, so the letters of undies are formed anew

parts.note: appears means is present or exists, read here as the verb is

explanation.surface: Something left unattended still turns up in a clean pair of knickers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fresh' rearranges the underwear into INDUSE, and 'in' puts the verb (appears, in the sense of being present) inside it after the D. 'yet' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has fallen out of use has been abandoned or left unattended.

clue.text: Ian's travelling with an ass, like an old Persian ruler

indicators.note: travelling suggests moving about, so these letters move into a new order

parts.note: the name Ian together with the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: A man named Ian journeys with a donkey, looking like an ancient Persian monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'travelling' shuffles IANS, AN and ASS. The Sassanians were the dynasty that ruled Persia from the third to the seventh century.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sassanian dynasty ruled the Persian empire before the Arab conquest, so the adjective describes its kings.

clue.text: Engaging costly clique, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells us the phrase is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: costly means high-priced and a clique is a ring, a closed group

explanation.surface: Joining an exclusive and expensive social circle, so the rumour goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'costly clique' gives HIGH RING, which said aloud matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Engaging staff means taking them on as employees.

clue.text: I'm to change into it? A take-off's called for!

parts.note: short for I am, giving the letters I and M

indicators.note: change means alter, so the letters of the words around it are rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor asks whether they must transform into something, since an impression is called for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' shuffles IM with INTO IT and A. 'to' and 's called for' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A take-off is a mocking copy of someone's manner, an impression.

clue.text: City girl brought up to be interpretive

indicators.note: in a down entry, brought up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: Lana is a girl's name

explanation.surface: An urban young woman raised to be analytical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' applies to the whole run: a down entry read upwards, so the city and the girl's name both come out backwards together.
explanation.definitionFit: Analytic means examining things by breaking them into parts, explaining or construing them.

clue.text: Getting us fuddled with wine isn't sensible

definitions.note: the phrase means is not prudent; the answer is the adjective, so read it as being not prudent

indicators.note: fuddled means muddled by drink, so the letters are confused

explanation.surface: Getting drunk on wine is a foolish idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fuddled' shuffles US and WINE, fittingly for a clue about drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Unwise means lacking good judgement, the opposite of prudent.

clue.text: Always leads to another?

parts.note: completes the saying about how events follow on from each other in a chain

explanation.walkthrough: The clue finishes the proverb about one event inevitably bringing about the next.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying goes that one item in a sequence leads on to a further item, so this phrase is its subject.

clue.text: A lot, for example, to be played smoothly

indicators.note: played here means toyed with, so the letters are moved about

parts.note: e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A musical direction saying a great deal is to be performed without breaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'played' shuffles A LOT and EG; 'to be' is a link. The surface reads as a musician's instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Legato is the musical direction for notes played in a smooth, connected way.

clue.text: Wrought iron panel — unmatched!

indicators.note: wrought means worked or shaped, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A craftsman praises a wrought-iron panel as peerless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrought' seems to describe the iron, but it signals that IRON and PANEL are worked into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonpareil means having no equal, peerless.

clue.text: Not a civil engineer at the present time

parts.note: non is a prefix meaning not

explanation.surface: Someone is currently out of work as an engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comes from the phrase 'for the nonce', meaning for now.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonce means the present occasion or purpose, as in the phrase for now only.

clue.text: Actual mayhem starting in this province

parts.note: real means actual, genuine

indicators.note: starting means only the beginning of the word mayhem is taken

explanation.surface: Real chaos breaks out in a region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting' takes the first letter of 'mayhem'; 'in this' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm is a kingdom or domain, a region or sphere of rule.

clue.text: Eyes watering in space, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly indicates that what is spoken is heard, giving a word that sounds alike

parts.note: room means space, as in room to move

explanation.surface: Someone's eyes are streaming while out in space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'space' gives ROOM, which said aloud matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheum is the watery discharge that runs from the eyes or nose.

clue.text: Travelling, is in a deserted area

indicators.note: travelling suggests moving about, so the letters move into a new order

explanation.surface: A traveller finds themselves in an empty wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Travelling' shuffles IS IN A. The definition is a pun: a deserted area is one that is a desert.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sinai peninsula between Egypt and Israel is largely desert, so it is an arid zone.

clue.text: The main, new advance in architectural design

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so the letters of the main are put into a new order

parts.note: on means forward, as in move on

explanation.surface: A main new development in building decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' shuffles THE MAIN into ANTHEMI, then ON (advance) is added. An anthemion is a honeysuckle-like ornament in Greek architecture.
explanation.definitionFit: An anthemion is a classical ornament of radiating leaves or petals used on buildings.

clue.text: More support needed, sadly, for men in Crete

indicators.note: sadly means badly or unfortunately, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Extra troops are required, unfortunately, for soldiers stationed in Crete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' shuffles FOR MEN IN CRETE; 'needed' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Reinforcement is additional strengthening, as with extra troops sent to back up a force.
